In Cold Blood. Truman Capote's 1966 novel is a true-crime narrative account of the 1959 murder of a Kansas farm family and the investigation leading to the capture and trial of the killers. Capote pioneered narrative nonfiction, blending meticulous journalism with literary technique to create a work that reads as both detective story and psychological study.

The Clutter family—Herb, Bonnie, Nancy, and Kenyon—are murdered in their rural Kansas home on November 15, 1959, apparently by burglars. The crime appears random; the killers seem to have no connection to the family and flee the state, leaving investigators with few leads. The investigation is painstaking and methodical. Two drifters, Richard Hickock and Perry Smith, are eventually identified through fingerprints and witness testimony.

Capote tracks the investigation alongside the killers, presenting their perspectives, childhoods, and psychological makeup as the mystery unfolds. The narrative builds to the capture of Hickock and Smith in Las Vegas, followed by their trial in Kansas. What emerges is extraordinary: the two men are partners in crime with starkly different personalities and motivations, yet bound together by their crime. Capote's immersion in the case and his literary technique have redefined the true-crime genre entirely. The novel concludes with their execution, offering neither judgment nor sentimentality, but a complex portrait of violence and human nature.
